checks.claim: Key: nitrogen is the solvent in air because it is the component present in the greatest amount (stem wording 'chemists count it as a solution' is safe at grade level)
checks.note: Grokipedia: nitrogen 'constitutes approximately 78% of the mixture and functions as the primary solvent'; solvent = 'the component present in the greater amount'. LibreTexts CK-12 16.01 agrees: air 'qualifies as a solution', '78% ... nitrogen, making it the solvent'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: oxygen (breathed by living things) is the solvent
checks.note: Oxygen is 20.95%, a solute; being breathed has nothing to do with being the solvent.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: water vapour, as water is the universal solvent
checks.note: Water vapour is 'near 0% to 4%' of air, a minor solute; 'universal solvent' refers to liquid water dissolving things.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: carbon dioxide, as it dissolves well in water
checks.note: CO2 is about 0.043% of air, a trace solute.

checks.claim: Context: air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen; oxygen, water vapour, argon and CO2 are the solutes
Context: water is the solvent in seawater because seawater is mostly water (about 96.5% water); air holds only a little water vapour
checks.note: Seawater is about 3.5% dissolved salt by weight, so the rest is water.

checks.claim: Context: brass is a solid solution, zinc spread through copper
checks.note: LibreTexts table: 'zinc in copper (brass alloy)'; Grokipedia Solution_(chemistry): 'brass, where zinc atoms substitute into the copper lattice'.

checks.claim: Stem: water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many substances; it holds salt in the sea, oxygen in a pond, and in blood carries nutrients
checks.note: USGS: water dissolves 'more substances than any other liquid', and 'Of course it cannot dissolve everything'; water moving through our bodies 'takes along valuable chemicals, minerals, and nutrients'. The stem does not claim water dissolves everything, so it is honest.

checks.claim: Key: its molecules have slightly charged ends (polar molecule)
checks.note: USGS: hydrogen side positive, oxygen side negative; water molecules pull the sodium and chloride ions apart. Grokipedia Properties_of_water: polar and ionic compounds dissolve readily.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it reacts with each thing it touches
checks.note: Dissolving is a physical change; water does not react with what it dissolves.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it is the only liquid that dissolves solids
checks.note: Ethanol dissolves solid iodine directly (tincture of iodine).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: its molecules are smaller than all others
checks.note: False as a reason and as a fact (helium, kinetic diameter 260 pm, is smaller than water, 265 pm).

checks.claim: Context: oxygen end slightly negative, hydrogen ends slightly positive; water tugs sodium and chloride apart
Context: alcohol dissolves the iodine in the tincture put on cuts
checks.note: About 2% iodine in about 50% ethanol; 'ethanol ... dissolving iodine directly'; applied to 'minor cuts, scrapes, and burns'.

checks.claim: Context: 'A hydrogen molecule is smaller than a water molecule'
checks.note: Depends on the measure of size. By kinetic diameter (the usual gas-molecule size) H2 is 289 pm and H2O only 265 pm, so water is the SMALLER; by van der Waals b (H2 0.0266, H2O 0.0305 L/mol, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waals_constants_(data_page)) and by mass H2 is smaller. A chemist could object. Fix: change the wrong choice to 'Its molecules are the lightest there are' and the context sentence to 'A hydrogen molecule weighs only a ninth as much as a water molecule, so that is not the reason.' (H2 = 2 u, H2O = 18 u; unambiguous).

checks.claim: Key: salt concentration rises as the same salt is in less water
checks.note: 'evaporation in warm, stagnant pools can elevate salinity to 50 ppt or higher'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it falls, as the salt goes off with the water
checks.note: Evaporation removes water only; in isolated pools it causes 'a relative increase in salinity'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: stays the same (no salt added); falls as the Sun's heat breaks the salt down
checks.note: Concentration depends on the water too; sunlight does not decompose sea salt.

checks.claim: Context: concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds
checks.note: 'the amount of solute per unit volume or mass of the solution'.

checks.claim: Context: seawater holds about 35 grams of salt in each kilogram
checks.note: 'typically averaging 35 grams of dissolved salts per kilogram of seawater (3.5 percent by weight)'.

checks.claim: Context: a sun-baked rock pool can reach 50 or more; rain dilutes the pool
checks.note: 50 ppt or higher by evaporation; rain can drop it 'below 30 ppt'. Race Rocks (racerocks.ca) reports a high pool evaporating to saturation.

checks.claim: Key: after dilution the flask holds the same amount of permanganate, spread through more water
checks.note: 'the concentration of a solute decreases upon addition of solvent, while the total amount of solute remains constant' (C1V1 = C2V2).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a tenth as much, as the colour is so pale
checks.note: The concentration is a tenth; the amount is unchanged.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: ten times as much (more liquid); less, as some has settled
checks.note: No solute is added; a true solution does not settle.

checks.claim: Stem: one 10 mL + 90 mL dilution turns a deep purple solution pale pink
checks.note: The writer's own source puts deep purple above about 10^-2 M and pale pink below about 10^-4 M: a hundredfold apart, so one tenfold step cannot take deep purple to pale pink. The classic school demo (https://www.teachoo.com/12518/3426/Activity---Show-Matter-is-Made-up-of-Particles/category/Extra-Questions/) repeats the same 10 mL into 90 mL step several times, each glass only a little paler, before the colour is very pale. Fix: stem 'the liquid turns a much paler purple'; wrong choice 'A tenth as much, as the colour is so much paler'. (Or make it 1 mL into 99 mL, a hundredfold, and change 'ten times'/'a tenth' in the context to 'a hundred times'/'a hundredth'.)

checks.claim: Context: same permanganate, ten times the liquid, a tenth the concentration, colour fades; a dissolved solute does not settle
checks.note: 10 mL made up to about 100 mL is a tenfold dilution.

checks.claim: Stem: potassium permanganate makes a deep purple solution
checks.note: 'intensely magenta-colored solution'; concentrated solutions 'deep purple'.

checks.claim: Key: the crushed grains dissolve first, as more surface meets the water
checks.note: 'A given quantity of solute dissolves faster when it is ground into small particles'; Grokipedia Solubility: more surface area increases the rate.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: the lump (weight drags it down); both at once (same mass); the lump (water seeps into its cracks)
checks.note: Rate depends on exposed surface, not mass or sinking; cracks expose far less surface than crushing.

checks.claim: Halite is the mineral form of sodium chloride, rock salt, and dissolves readily
checks.note: 'Halite, commonly known as rock salt, is the naturally occurring mineral form of sodium chloride'; about 35.9 g per 100 mL at 25 C.

checks.claim: Stem: a fist-sized lump in a beaker of water will be 'gone'
checks.note: A fist is about 250 mL (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4976119/table/tab02); at halite's density of about 2.17 g/cm3 that is roughly 540 g of salt, which needs about 1.5 litres of water (35.9 g per 100 mL) before it can all dissolve. In an ordinary beaker the water saturates and neither the lump nor the grains is ever gone. Fix: 'a walnut-sized lump' (about 40 g, needs about 110 mL), or say 'a large tank of water'.

checks.claim: Context: water works only where it touches the solid; crushing bares more surface
Key: hot water's particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
checks.note: 'Heating up a solvent gives the molecules more kinetic energy'; they 'collide with the solute with greater frequency'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the heat melts the crystal into a blue liquid first
checks.note: The pentahydrate does not melt in hot water; on dry heating it loses water (63, 109, 200 C) and decomposes rather than melting (anhydrous about 590 C). Grokipedia Copper(II)_sulfate: dehydrates 'rather than melting'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the heat turns the crystal into a new substance
checks.note: Dissolving is a physical change at this grade's level.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: water's particles grow bigger and push the crystal apart
checks.note: Heated matter expands by greater average separation of particles, not bigger particles.

checks.claim: Copper sulfate forms blue crystals
checks.note: 'bright blue triclinic crystals or granules'; solubility rises markedly with temperature.

checks.claim: Context: dissolves rather than melts; no new substance; particles stay the same size
Stem: Epsom salt is the crystal used in soaks for sore muscles
checks.note: MgSO4.7H2O 'known as Epsom salt', colourless crystals, about 710 g/L at 20 C; used in baths to 'ease muscle aches'. The stem says only that it is used so, not that it works.

checks.claim: Key: stirring keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
checks.note: Unstirred, 'the water right at the surface of the solute becomes saturated'; stirring brings fresh solvent. Grokipedia Solubility: agitation thins 'the hydrodynamic boundary layer adjacent to the solute surface'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it splits the salt's particles into smaller bits
checks.note: Wrong as written: the salt's particles are not split. Mild caution only: a reader who takes 'particles' as grains could argue a stirring rod grinds crystals; the bank's use of 'particles' (as in the copper sulfate question) is the tiny particles, so it stands.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it lets the water hold more salt in all
checks.note: 'neither stirring nor breaking up a solute affect the overall amount of solute that dissolves'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it mixes in air, and the air dissolves the salt
checks.note: Air does not dissolve salt.

checks.claim: Context: saturated layer next to the crystal; stirring changes the rate, not how much can dissolve; no particle split
Stem: potassium nitrate is a white salt; undissolved crystals mean the solution is saturated
checks.note: Infobox 'white solid'; Grokipedia Potassium_nitrate 'white to dirty gray crystalline solid'. Grokipedia Solubility: saturated = 'in dynamic equilibrium with any undissolved solute'.

checks.claim: Key: warming the water gets more of the crystals to dissolve
checks.note: 'potassium nitrate rises sharply from 31.6 g/100 g at 20 C to 245 g/100 g at 100 C'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: stirring faster; crushing to a powder; leaving it to stand for days
checks.note: 'neither stirring nor breaking up a solute affect the overall amount of solute that dissolves'; a saturated solution at a fixed temperature takes no more however long it stands (standing would if anything evaporate water).

checks.claim: Context: water near boiling holds more than seven times as much potassium nitrate as water at 20 C
checks.note: Wikipedia 316 g/L at 20 C, 2439 g/L at 100 C (7.7x); Grokipedia 31.6 to 245 g/100 g (7.8x); chemister.ru 31.6 to 243.6 g/100 g water (7.7x, https://chemister.ru/Databases/Chemdatabase/properties-en.php?id=513).

checks.claim: Context: warmer water holds more of most solids
Key: as the pond warms from 20 to 30 C the oxygen it can hold falls; warm water holds less gas
checks.note: Gas solubility 'generally decreases with increasing temperature, as higher thermal energy favors the escape of gas molecules from the solution'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: rises; stays the same as only solids change; drops to none as the gas boils away
checks.note: It falls only from about 9.1 to 7.6 mg/L, nowhere near zero.

checks.claim: Context: about 9 mg/L at 20 C and about 7.6 mg/L at 30 C in fresh water
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 9 mg/L at 20 C, 7.6 mg/L at 30 C; Engineering Toolbox table: 9.1 and 7.6 mg/L at 1 atm.

checks.claim: Context: hot, calm summer weather can leave pond fish short of oxygen; cold tumbling streams hold plenty
checks.note: USGS: 'Cold water can hold more dissolved oxygen than warm water'; 'a period of hot, calm weather, resulting in the loss of many fish'.

checks.claim: Stem: fish breathe oxygen dissolved in the water
Stem: CO2 forced into chilled water under pressure and capped
checks.note: Water chilled to about 0-5 C; CO2 injected at about 3-6 bar.

checks.claim: Key: the pressure drops, so less gas can stay dissolved
checks.note: Henry's law: dissolved CO2 proportional to its partial pressure; 'the sudden pressure drop leads to supersaturation ... dissolved CO2 forms bubbles'. The bubbles are carbon dioxide.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the pressure drops, so the water starts to boil
checks.note: At ordinary air pressure water boils at 100 C; cold or room-temperature water does not boil.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: air rushes in and reacts with the water; air rushes in and forms the bubbles
checks.note: Gas rushes out on opening; the fizz is dissolved CO2 escaping 'as pressure drops and the gas escapes'.

checks.claim: Context: more pressure, more gas held; opening drops pressure to that of ordinary air; the water is far too cold to boil

unit_notes: 7 ok, 1 error, 2 uncertain. Error 608fb33e6e: one tenfold dilution cannot turn deep purple permanganate pale pink (the writer's own source puts the two a hundredfold apart); say 'a much paler purple'. Uncertain 40838f3bd0: 'a hydrogen molecule is smaller than a water molecule' depends on the measure (kinetic diameter H2 289 pm > H2O 265 pm); use weight instead. Uncertain cc90c4c8ff: a fist-sized lump (about 540 g) needs about 1.5 L of water to dissolve at all; make it walnut-sized. Air as a solution, the universal-solvent context (honest: it never says water dissolves everything), the tide pool, KNO3 (7.7x), O2 at 20/30 C and the CO2 fizz all check out.
